title: Traditional Board Games of the Region
summary: How simple board games played with seeds and holes in the sand have tested players' strategy and skill across the Arab world and Africa for centuries, with no dice and no luck involved.
poll: A simple game with no fancy pieces can be just as fun as an expensive one.

versions.title: Games with Seeds and Holes
versions.text:
Across the region, folks play a game with seeds and holes. It is a very old game. You need no dice. You just need to think.

The board has rows of small holes. Seeds sit in each hole. Players move seeds from hole to hole.

The goal is to get more seeds than the next player. Think ahead to win.

You do not need fancy things to play. Dig holes in sand. Use seeds or small stones.

No dice are used. It is all about skill.

This game is very old. Folks in many lands play it. It has many names.

All can play. Just find seeds, holes, and a friend.

versions.title: Traditional Board Games of the Region
versions.text:
Across the region, people play a board game using seeds and small holes. This old game needs no dice and no luck at all. To win, a player must think ahead.

The board has two rows of small holes, called pits. Seeds sit inside each pit. On a turn, a player picks up the seeds from one pit and drops them, one by one, into the next pits.

The goal is to capture more seeds than the other player. A player wins seeds by landing the last seed in just the right pit. A good player thinks several moves ahead.

You do not need fancy things to play this game. People dig small holes in the sand or carve them into wood. Seeds, stones, or date pits can be used as pieces.

No dice are used in this game, and luck plays no part. It is all about skill, patience, and good thinking.

This game is very old, maybe one of the oldest games on Earth. In English, it is often called mancala, but it has many other names across the region.

Anyone can play, too. Just find some seeds, a few small holes, and a friend.

wrong.C: This game is usually played by two opponents.

MID.prompt: Explain why strategy matters more than luck in this ancient game. Use at least two key words.
checklist: I explained what strategy means in this game.
I explained why there is no luck involved.
MID.modelAnswer: Strategy matters more than luck in this ancient game because no dice are used, so every win depends on how well a player plans against the opponent. A skilled player studies the pits across the region's boards and thinks several moves ahead to capture more seeds than the opponent.

keyWords.definition: easy for anyone to use, reach, or take part in
keyWords.example: The park is accessible to everyone in the neighborhood.

keyWords.definition: to work something out carefully, often with numbers or steps
keyWords.example: She tried to calculate how long the trip would take.

keyWords.definition: customs, art, and traditions passed down from earlier generations
keyWords.example: Traditional music is part of our family's heritage.

keyWords.definition: a slightly different form of the same basic thing
keyWords.example: Each region has its own variation of the recipe.

keyWords.definition: found or happening over a large area
keyWords.example: Rain was widespread across the whole country that week.

questions.stem: Which statement best summarizes the article?
options: An ancient, purely strategic game remains widespread today.
A newly invented game has quickly replaced older board games everywhere.
Only wealthy households can afford to play this traditional game.
This game depends mostly on rolling dice and guessing correctly.
questions.why: The article explains how this ancient, skill-based game remains widespread and accessible using only simple materials.

wrong.B: The article says the game is ancient, not newly invented.
wrong.C: The article stresses that no costly equipment is needed.
wrong.D: The article says no dice are used and chance plays no part.

questions.stem: According to the article, what makes this game accessible to nearly anyone?
options: It can only be purchased at specialty game shops
It only needs simple seeds, stones, and sand holes
It requires an expensive, professionally built board
It can only be learned from one certified teacher
questions.why: The article says using seeds, stones, and holes in the sand or wood makes the game accessible to nearly anyone.

wrong.A: Game shops are not mentioned in the article.
wrong.C: The article says no costly board is required.
wrong.D: No certified teacher is mentioned in the article.

questions.stem: What must a player calculate during a turn?
options: The total weight of all the stones in play
The gap between the board and nearest wall
The right pit for landing the final seed
The exact count of dice rolled by the foe
questions.why: The article explains that a player calculates landing the final seed in a pit holding just the right number of seeds.

wrong.A: Weight of stones is not discussed in the article.
wrong.B: Distance to a wall is not part of the game.
wrong.D: No dice are rolled in this game.

questions.stem: Why does a skilled player try to anticipate the opponent's next move?
options: To plan a better move and capture more seeds
To end the match as quickly as can be done
To avoid ever using any seeds at all
To make the game board larger during play
questions.why: The article says anticipating the opponent's move helps a player plan and capture more seeds, which is the goal.

wrong.B: Ending quickly is not described as the goal.
wrong.C: Seeds must be used to play the game at all.
wrong.D: Board size does not change during play.

questions.stem: Which detail best supports the idea that this game is part of a rich regional heritage?
options: The board has two long rows of small pits
Regions use their own names, such as kharbga
A player picks up seeds from one pit at a time
Seeds get dropped one by one into pits
questions.why: Having many local names across different regions shows the game has long been woven into different cultures' heritage.

wrong.A: This describes the board, not heritage.
wrong.C: This describes a rule, not cultural heritage.
wrong.D: This describes how seeds move, not heritage.

questions.stem: How is this ancient game similar across the Arab world and Africa, despite regional variation?
options: Every single region uses the exact same local name
Only one region is allowed to use seeds as pieces
The core goal of capturing seeds stays the same
Each region uses a wholly different board shape
questions.why: Even though local names and small details vary by region, the article shows the core strategic goal remains the same everywhere.

wrong.A: The article says local names actually differ by region.
wrong.B: Seeds are used as pieces in many regions, not just one.
wrong.D: The article does not describe totally different board shapes.

questions.stem: What can be inferred from the fact that this game needs no dice and no luck?
options: The game rewards careful thought over chance
The game cannot ever be enjoyed by beginners
The game ends up with no clear winner at all
The game was designed only for professionals
questions.why: Since every win depends on skill and strategy rather than chance, careful thought is clearly rewarded over luck.

wrong.B: The article does not say beginners cannot enjoy it.
wrong.C: The player with more seeds wins the game.
wrong.D: The article says anyone can play, not just professionals.

questions.stem: How is the article organized?
options: As an argument that modern games beat old ones
By how the game is played, then its history
As a set of safety rules for playing near sand
As a biography of the game's single inventor
questions.why: The article moves from explaining how the game is played, to the simple materials used, to its ancient history and spread.

wrong.A: The article does not rank modern games above old ones.
wrong.C: No safety rules are given in the article.
wrong.D: No single inventor is named in the article.

HIGH.prompt: Explain how this game's accessible materials helped it become part of a widespread regional heritage. Use at least two key words.
checklist: I explained what makes the game accessible.
I explained how it became widespread across the region.
I used at least two key words.
HIGH.modelAnswer: This game's accessible materials, like seeds, stones, and simple holes dug in sand, allowed it to spread easily, since no one needed costly equipment to play. Over centuries, this helped the game become part of a widespread heritage across the Arab world and Africa, even as each region developed its own small variation and local name for the same strategic game.
